archetype.name: Retooling (pass-first, leaky defense)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff has turned last year's worst offense into a functional, Cousins-led passing attack, but a non-existent run game and a defense that wins on pressure and takeaways rather than down-to-down stops leave it a .500-type team at best.

report.headline: The passing revival is real; the takeaway-fueled 3-0 start was not.
report.take:
Start with how far this offense has come. A year ago the Raiders ranked last in offensive EPA (-0.192) and scored 14.2 points a game. Under Klint Kubiak, with Kirk Cousins starting all seven games, they score 26.1 a game (6th) and rank 9th in pass EPA per play. That is a real structural change, built on a pass game that has produced positive EPA in six of seven weeks. The protection holds up, too: a 3.5% sack rate ranks 4th. The ball is spread among tight ends and backs. Brock Bowers leads the team in targets despite playing only five games, and Michael Mayer and Ashton Jeanty soak up heavy volume.

The rest of the roster is not built the same way. The run game is close to broken. Backs average 1.4 yards before contact (32nd), the run success rate is 32nd, and every single game has posted negative rush EPA. This is a line problem, not a game-script one. The defense is a strange mix. It generates the 2nd-best pressure rate in the league and has 12 takeaways (2nd), yet it ranks 27th in success rate allowed, 32nd in EPA on short passes, 31st in explosive run rate and 30th in red-zone touchdown rate. It harasses quarterbacks and forces mistakes, but when the ball comes out quickly or goes on the ground, it bleeds yards and points.

That split explains the season's two halves. The 3-0 start came against Miami, the Chargers and New Orleans, three offenses that rank in the bottom half today. The defense produced most of the season's takeaways in those games. Since then the turnovers have dried up, with zero against Kansas City and Buffalo, and the defense has allowed 30-plus points in every game. Rams, Patriots and Chiefs ground games have run through it. The point differential says this is a 2.7-win team, roughly what the record says, so there is no hidden luck either way. Covering five of seven spreads (1st ATS) mostly reflects how low the market priced a team coming off a 3-14 season.

Where it goes from here depends on whether the pass rush can keep generating turnovers, because nothing else on defense is reliable. The offense should travel, but the back half of the schedule is loaded with top-10 defenses, and an offense with no run game is easier to squeeze once a defense can play two-high and rally to the short stuff.

strengths.title: A genuinely efficient passing offense
strengths.body: Cousins has the Raiders 9th in pass EPA per play and 6th in scoring, a complete reversal from last year's 32nd-ranked offense. The production is durable: passing EPA was positive in every game until the Rams, including 365 yards against Kansas City's top-five defense. A clean pocket helps, since the sack rate allowed ranks 4th even with a mediocre 16th-ranked pressure rate. This is the most sustainable part of the team.

strengths.title: Elite pressure that creates turnovers
strengths.body: The front gets home: the pressure rate ranks 2nd and the QB hit rate 4th. That pressure has driven 12 takeaways and a +4 turnover margin. Pressure is a stable skill, so the rush should keep producing. Takeaways themselves are streaky, as their absence in two of the last four games shows, so expect fewer of them.

concerns.title: Run game is broken at the line
concerns.body: Backs get 1.4 yards before contact, worst in the league, and the stuff rate and run EPA both rank 31st. Jeanty's 106 carries have mostly been wasted downs. This is blocking, not script, because rush EPA was negative even in the comfortable early wins. It makes the offense one-dimensional and puts every drive on Cousins's arm.

concerns.title: Defense collapses without turnovers
concerns.body: Strip out the takeaways and this defense rarely gets stops. It ranks 32nd against short passes, 31st in explosive runs allowed and 30th in red-zone touchdown rate, which is how it gives up 28.1 points a game (29th). The recent ground damage (199 rushing yards to the Rams, 189 to the Chiefs) shows a front that rushes the passer well but misses tackles and gives up chunk runs. This is a real flaw, not noise.

concerns.title: Record matches a below-average team
concerns.body: The point differential implies 2.7 wins and net EPA ranks 23rd. The 3-4 record is neither unlucky nor fortunate; it is what a team with a good offense and a bad defense earns. The league-best cover rate says more about low expectations than about hidden quality.

trend.note: They won the first three behind a flood of takeaways against weak offenses, then lost every game since as the turnovers dried up and the defense allowed 30-plus each week. The Rams game was the first in which the passing offense also went negative.

nextGame.headline: Pick'em at the Jets: Cousins's arm against a sack-prone line
nextGame.body:
The Book has the Jets as 1.5-point home favorites with a 45.5 total, essentially a coin flip. The matchups lean the Raiders' way through the air. The Jets rank 25th in pass EPA allowed but 7th against the run, which pushes Kubiak toward what he does well anyway, and the Jets give up a lot underneath (27th in short-pass EPA). On the other side, Geno Smith plays behind a line that ranks 28th in sack rate, a dangerous spot against a Raiders pass rush that ranks 2nd in pressure rate. The Jets' offense is middle-of-the-pack in efficiency (15th) but scores only 19.6 a game.

Availability tilts toward Las Vegas. The Jets are without running back Breece Hall, backup back Kene Nwangwu and guard Dylan Parham, and edge Joseph Ossai is out. DT T'Vondre Sweat is questionable after leaving last week. Losing Hall and Parham thins an already weak run game (28th in yards before contact) and a leaky interior. For the Raiders, receivers Dont'e Thornton Jr. and tight end Carter Runyon remain on IR, while Jack Bech has been designated to return. Neither changes much with the passing game running through the tight ends.

waysToWin.title: Throw it at the Jets' soft middle
waysToWin.body: The Jets defend the run well and the pass poorly, and they have held opposing WR1s well under their averages, so the matchup favors the Raiders' tight-end-heavy distribution. Bowers and Mayer working the short and intermediate middle against a defense ranked 27th on short passes is the cleanest path to points. Leaning pass-heavy here is the correct read, not a gamble.

waysToWin.title: Pass rush feasts on a leaky line
waysToWin.body: The Jets have allowed 21 sacks and an 8.7% sack rate, and they now play without guard Dylan Parham and their top back. With Hall out, the Jets will lean on Smith in obvious passing downs, which is exactly where this Raiders front lives. Sacks and strip chances are the Raiders' most likely source of the short fields that won them September.

waysToWin.title: Win the close finish
waysToWin.body: The Jets have won only 20% of their one-score games and commit 8.3 penalties a game, 25th in the league. If this stays tight into the fourth quarter, the Jets' history of late mistakes gives an efficient Raiders passing offense room to steal it.

waysToLose.title: Dead run game invites the blitz
waysToLose.body: Against a run defense ranked 7th, Jeanty's carries will likely go nowhere, leaving Cousins in long-yardage downs. The Jets' sack rate ranks 5th even with an average pressure rate, so they finish when they get home. A few drive-killing sacks on third-and-long could leave the Raiders kicking field goals while the Jets cash in.

waysToLose.title: Red-zone and short-pass leaks
waysToLose.body: The Raiders give up touchdowns on 78.6% of red-zone trips and are the league's worst defense against short throws. Smith can neutralize the pass rush with quick game, and a Jets offense that struggles to score could suddenly turn into a 24-point team. If the defense can't force turnovers, it has shown no other way to get off the field.

waysToLose.title: Chunk runs even without Hall
waysToLose.body: The Raiders allow explosive runs at the second-worst rate in the league and have just given up big rushing days to the Rams, Patriots and Chiefs. Even a depleted Jets backfield can find big gains against a defense that misses tackles at the second level.

nextGame.watch: The Raiders' sack and turnover count against Geno Smith: if the pass rush produces takeaways, the Raiders likely win; if Smith gets the ball out quickly underneath, this defense has no answer.

restOfSeason.body:
The passing offense is real and should keep this team competitive in shootouts, but expect the scoring to slide. Five of the remaining nine opponents (San Francisco, Seattle, Denver twice and Cleveland) plus Kansas City rank top-10 on defense, and an offense with no run game is easier to scheme against. The defense's pressure should hold up, but the takeaway pace that carried September is unlikely to return, and the underlying stop rate points to more 28-point afternoons than 14-point ones.

The soft spots on the calendar are the Chargers, Tennessee and Arizona at the back end, plus this week's coin flip with the Jets. Those are the realistic wins. Against the top half of the schedule, the Raiders will need the pass rush to win a game or two on its own. That projects to a final record in the 6-8 range: a clear step up from 3-14 and a real foundation on offense, but not a playoff team.
swingFactors: Whether the pass rush keeps producing turnovers
Any life in the run game against top-10 fronts

confidence.note: Seven-game sample, but the pass/run and pressure/coverage splits are consistent week to week.
